parts.title: A Volunteer Conservation Week
parts.scenario: A British woman phones a Canadian conservation organisation to enquire about a volunteer week of trail repair and wildlife surveys in a national park.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Greg
voices.desc: Volunteer coordinator — male, 40s, relaxed, friendly, outdoorsy; Canadian accent (en-CA)

voices.label: Helen
voices.desc: Caller — female, early 30s, polite, curious, a little self-deprecating; British accent (en-GB)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning an organisation to ask about a volunteer conservation holiday. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [a phone line clicks open] [warm, easy-going] Good afternoon, Northwood Conservation Volunteers, Greg speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [polite, slightly hesitant] Oh, hello. I'm calling from England, actually, so, um, sorry if there's a bit of a delay on the line. I saw your website and I'm interested in one of the volunteer weeks in the national park.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [friendly] No problem at all, you're coming through fine. You'd be looking at Kettle Ridge, then. That's the only park we're working in this summer.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [relieved] Yes, that's the one. Could you tell me a bit about what the volunteers actually do? The website was a little bit vague.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [light laugh] Yeah, we keep meaning to update it. So basically there are two parts to it. Half the time you're out on the trails doing repairs, and the rest of the time you're helping our ecologists with wildlife surveys.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [interested] What kind of wildlife? I read something about birds.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [explaining] Right, that'd be the old page. For years the surveys were all about songbirds, counting nests, that kind of thing. And people still ask about the beavers, because they're kind of famous out there. But this season the funding's come through to study bats, so that's what all the survey work is focused on.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [delighted] Oh, I'd love that, actually. And the trail work, is that very heavy?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [reassuring, but honest] It's physical, I won't pretend it isn't. The park's had a lot of erosion. Last year the volunteers rebuilt the boardwalks across the wetland, so those are done. This year it's mainly the steeper sections up the ridge, where the old wooden steps have rotted, so you'd be pulling those out and putting new ones in.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [thoughtful] Right. OK. [short pause] And dates. I'm fairly flexible, but July would suit me best.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [typing, murmuring] July, let me pull that up. [normal voice] So each week runs Sunday to Saturday. The week starting the fifth is full, I'm afraid.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [hopeful] What about the twelfth?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [checking, then apologetic] The twelfth... I've got one place left. Oh, no, hang on, somebody reserved that this morning. Sorry about that. But the week beginning the nineteenth has plenty of room.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [decisive] The nineteenth, then. That's better, actually, because I've got a wedding on the twelfth anyway. [chuckles] I don't know why I suggested it.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [laughs] Fair enough. Now, cost. The standard fee is five hundred and sixty dollars for the week. That covers your accommodation, all your meals and transport inside the park.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [checking] Is that Canadian dollars?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [matter-of-fact] Canadian, yes. There is a reduced rate of four hundred and twenty for full-time students.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [wry] Ah. I finished university about ten years ago, so I don't think that one applies to me.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [good-humoured] Afraid not. And accommodation: a lot of people assume they'll be camping in tents, but we stopped doing that a few years back after some, ah, encounters with the local bears.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [alarmed laugh] Right!

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [chuckling] So now everyone stays in a bunkhouse near the ranger station. There are a couple of log cabins on the site as well, but those are for the staff, unfortunately.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [amused] A bunkhouse. That sounds very Canadian.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [practical] So, packing. We'll email you a full list, but just so you know, we provide work gloves, hard hats and all the tools. Bedding's provided too, so you won't need a sleeping bag.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [making a note] Good, that saves on luggage. What about equipment for the bat surveys? Do I need anything special?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [explaining] The bat detectors, the electronic gadgets that pick up their calls, we lend you those. They're expensive and pretty delicate. But we've only got a few pairs of binoculars, and they're always in demand, so we do ask volunteers to bring their own.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [thinking aloud] I've got an old pair somewhere in the loft. [brisk] And do I need to be especially fit?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [candid] Reasonably. The guidance used to say you had to manage twenty kilometres a day on foot, which put a lot of people off, and frankly most days we weren't doing anything like that. So now we say you need to be comfortable hiking about twelve kilometres a day, with a pack.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [confident] Twelve's fine. I do a lot of walking at home.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [businesslike] Great. And in terms of paperwork, you don't need any first-aid qualification, all our team leaders are trained, but we do need a reference from your employer or a tutor, just saying you're reliable.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [cheerful] I can get one from my manager, no problem. Now, how would I actually get to the park? I'm assuming I'd fly into Toronto?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [explaining] Most people do, yeah. Then you'd take the train north. We used to pick people up at the airport, but it was a five-hour drive each way, so we don't do that any more. Instead there's a free shuttle bus from the train station in Pellatt.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [unsure] Sorry, could you spell that?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [slowly, spelling each letter clearly] Sure. P... E... double L... A... T... T.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [repeating slowly, as if writing it down] P, E, double L, A, double T. Got it.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [helpful] The shuttle leaves at four on the Sunday afternoon, so you'd want to be on the morning train.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [thinking] OK. And is there any free time during the week, or is it all work?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [upbeat] There's free time most evenings, and on the final day there's an optional trip. It used to be a boat cruise on the lake, but the operator went out of business, so now it's a canoe trip with one of the rangers. That's forty dollars extra. Or if you'd prefer, there's a guided hike that's free, but honestly, most people have had enough of hiking by then.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [laughs] I can imagine. I'll go for the canoe trip, I think. [short pause] So what's the next step?

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [wrapping up, friendly] I'll send you an application form by email. If I could just take your name and email address?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [clearly] It's Helen Marsh, and the email is helen dot marsh at our mail dot com, all one word.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [reading back] Helen dot marsh at ourmail dot com. Perfect. You should get that within the hour.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: [warm] Brilliant. Thanks so much, Greg, you've been really helpful.

script.speaker: Greg
script.text: [cheerful] My pleasure. Hope we see you in July. Bye now.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

question_groups.instructions: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.title: Ashcombe Botanic Garden
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (1 speaker)
parts.scenario: A volunteer guide welcomes a group of visitors to a botanical garden, explains the map and describes what is happening in each glasshouse.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Marion
voices.desc: Volunteer guide — female, 60s, warm, enthusiastic, slightly projecting to a small group; British accent (en-GB)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a talk to a group of visitors at a botanical garden. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [faint chatter of a small group fading] [warm, welcoming, projecting slightly] Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe Botanic Garden. My name's Marion, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you head off and explore, I'll give you a quick introduction so you can make the most of your visit.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [practical] You should all have a copy of the map, which I'll talk you through in a moment. We're standing in the Visitor Centre, which is just inside the main entrance, on the left as you come in. The shop's in here too, so if you want to buy seeds or gifts, this is the place.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [clear, guiding] Now, if you look straight across the main path, directly opposite us, you'll see a low brick building with a green door. A lot of people assume that's another shop and wander in asking for packets of seeds. [light laugh] It isn't. That's our Seed Bank, where we store seeds from over four thousand species. It's open to the public every morning, and there's a small exhibition inside.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [brisk] Next, the café. If you were here a few years ago, you might remember it beside the lake, on the west shore. Well, it isn't there any more. That building was far too small. The new café is on Lime Avenue, which is the long, straight path running east from the lake towards the Walled Garden. As you walk along it, the café's on your right, so on the south side, about halfway along. [light] You can't miss it; there's a big terrace.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [cheerful, a little louder] Families, this is for you. The children's trail, which is a sort of treasure hunt with twelve wooden animals to find, used to begin here at the Visitor Centre, and I'm afraid the leaflet still says it does. [apologetic] The leaflets were printed before we changed things.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [clear] It now starts from that old café building I mentioned, on the western shore of the lake, right where the woodland begins. The trail then winds through the trees up to the bird hide in the north-west corner. So that's where it finishes, not where it starts.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [enthusiastic] Then there are our bees. We have six hives, and people often expect to find them in the Walled Garden, among all the flowers. [chuckles] And they used to be there, but they were a bit too close to the visitors for comfort. So they've moved to a quiet spot behind the Palm House. Go round the back of it and you'll find them right up against the northern boundary wall. There's a viewing screen, so you can watch them safely.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [measured, regretful] The little building right next to the Palm House, on its eastern side, is the Victorian fernery. Sadly, that's closed this year while the roof is repaired, so please don't try to go in.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [clear] And finally on the map, the Herb Garden. It's inside the Walled Garden, at the far end of Lime Avenue. Just before you go through the gate, on your left, there's a fenced area full of bins and heaps. That's our composting demonstration. Don't stop there! Go through the gate and carry on to the far right-hand corner, the north-eastern corner, and that's where the herbs are. [warm] It smells wonderful at this time of year.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [shifting to a new topic, brightly] Now let me tell you about our glasshouses, because each one has something a bit special going on at the moment.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [proud] The biggest, of course, is the Palm House. It's over a hundred and fifty years old, and it's home to some enormous palms and banana plants. [apologetic laugh] People always ask if they can try the bananas. I'm afraid you can't. They aren't really grown for eating. What you can do, though, is climb the spiral staircase to the gallery that runs right round the top of the building. From up there you're level with the crowns of the palms. It's quite a view.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [lighter, informative] Much smaller is the Alpine House. Alpine plants are tiny, so they're easy to overlook. We've put hand lenses on chains along the benches, so you can get a really close look at the flowers. Some are only a few millimetres across. [matter-of-fact] The Alpine House is also where we used to run our potting classes, but there wasn't enough room, so they've moved. I'll come back to that in a moment.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [excited, dropping her voice slightly] In the Desert House we have something of a celebrity. It's an agave, sometimes called the century plant, which was planted back in nineteen seventy-one and had never flowered. Until this month. It's sent up a flower spike nearly eight metres tall, and it won't happen again, because agaves die after flowering. So don't miss it.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [slightly wistful] Some of you may remember Arthur, the volunteer who used to give talks in the Desert House about the history of the glasshouses. He retired last spring, unfortunately, so if that's what you're interested in, you'll need the guidebook.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [informative] The Orchid House is kept very warm and humid, so you might want to take your coat off. Vanilla is actually an orchid, and visitors sometimes ask whether they can taste the vanilla we grow. [light laugh] Sadly not. Our vines are still far too young to produce pods.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [engaged, explaining] But the scientists there are working on some very rare orchids, and because the insects that normally pollinate them don't live in this country, the team has to do that job themselves, with a tiny paintbrush. On weekday mornings you can watch them at work through the window of the laboratory.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [warm, amused] And finally, the Water-lily House, with the giant lilies whose leaves can be two metres across. In Victorian times they used to sit small children on the leaves to show how strong they were. [chuckles] We don't do that any more, before anyone asks!

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [clear, inviting] But this is now where those potting classes I mentioned take place. Every afternoon at two o'clock there's a free half-hour session where you can learn how to take cuttings and pot up a plant to take home. There's no need to book; just turn up.

script.speaker: Marion
script.text: [wrapping up, friendly] Right, I think that's everything. Do enjoy your visit!

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

question_groups.instructions: Label the map below. Write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 11–15.
question_groups.heading: Ashcombe Botanic Garden
question_groups.layout: Plan of a rectangular garden, north at the top. The Main Entrance is in the middle of the south (bottom) edge, with a Car Park outside it to the bottom right. A Main Path runs straight north from the Main Entrance to a large oval Lake in the centre of the garden. Just inside the entrance, on the WEST (left) side of the Main Path, is the labelled Visitor Centre. The western half of the garden north of the Visitor Centre is labelled Woodland. On the north side of the Lake is a large labelled building, the Palm House. Lime Avenue (labelled) is a straight path running east from the east shore of the Lake to the gate of the Walled Garden (labelled), a square enclosure occupying the north-east corner of the garden. Letters: A — a small building on the EAST side of the Main Path, directly opposite the Visitor Centre. B — a small building on the WEST shore of the Lake, at the edge of the Woodland. C — a small area immediately NORTH of (behind) the Palm House, against the northern boundary wall. D — a small building attached to the EAST side of the Palm House. E — inside the Walled Garden, in its far north-east corner. F — on the SOUTH side of Lime Avenue, about halfway along. G — on the NORTH side of Lime Avenue, just outside the Walled Garden gate. H — in the Woodland, in the north-west corner of the garden.

parts.title: Placements in a Theatre Costume Department
parts.scenario: Two drama students, Freya and Callum, evaluate the work placements they did in the costume department of a regional theatre and plan a presentation.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Freya
voices.desc: Student — female, about 21, thoughtful, articulate, quietly decisive; light Southern English accent (en-GB)

voices.label: Callum
voices.desc: Student — male, about 22, lively, quick to react, often changes his mind; deeper voice, Northern English accent (en-GB)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two drama students, Freya and Callum, discussing the work placements they did in the costume department of a theatre. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [friendly, settling in] So, shall we make a start on this evaluation? It's due on Friday, and I'd quite like to get the presentation sorted out as well.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [easy-going] Yeah, go on. The form says reasons for choosing the placement first.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [light laugh] Well, you'll have to do that bit, because I didn't really have a choice. It was the only one left by the time I applied. Why did you go for costume? I always thought you were set on doing set design.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [thinking back] So did I, to be honest. And Dr Harmon did say costume might suit me better, because of my essay on fashion history, but I didn't take much notice at the time. What actually made up my mind was finding out the Riverside Playhouse was putting on that Restoration comedy. I'm completely obsessed with seventeenth-century clothes.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [teasing] And there was me thinking it was because your nan taught you to sew.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [chuckles] Well, she did, and it came in handy once I was there, but no, that's not why I applied.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [brisk] OK. First impressions next.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [animated] I remember being amazed by how early everything had to be ready. Finished costumes two whole weeks before the first night!

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [measured] Mm, that didn't surprise me so much. Our lecturer had warned us about it. And I knew it'd be a small team, so there being only four of them wasn't a shock either. What really took me aback was the store room. I'd assumed they made everything from scratch for each show, but most of what they used had been worn before, in earlier productions, and was just altered and re-trimmed.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [agreeing, amused] Yeah, some of those coats must have been in about thirty plays.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [moving on] And then there's the section on supervision. Lorna, basically.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [a little grumbling] I mean, she's brilliant, but I did think she asked too much of us sometimes. Expecting us to finish a whole bodice in a day...

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [disagreeing, gently] I don't think that's fair. She never asked for anything she hadn't shown us first. If anything, I'd say she was better with a needle than with words. She'd just do things rather than explain them.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [firm] No, I can't agree with that. Her explanations were really clear. It's just that she talked incredibly fast.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [conceding, laughing] Fair enough. But one thing we definitely agree on is that she trusted us with far more than I'd expected. I was altering a costume for the lead actor in my second week!

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [warmly] Absolutely. I never thought they'd let me anywhere near the main cast.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [sighs] Now, difficulties. For me, the hardest thing at first was the jargon. Toiles, basques, breaking down. I had to keep a glossary in the back of my notebook.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [shrugging] That didn't bother me. I'd picked most of it up from Nan. The evening shifts were what got me... [correcting himself] actually, no, they weren't too bad once I'd got used to them. I'm a night owl anyway.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [thoughtful] I didn't mind them at all. I liked being there during the show. But what we both struggled with was the reflective log.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [groans] Oh, don't. I was writing up three days at a time on a Sunday night.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [rueful] Same. There just wasn't a spare moment in the day to sit down and write anything.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [moving on] OK, and the presentation. I wondered about comparing costume for the stage with costume for film.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [doubtful] Neither of us has done any film work, though. We'd just be guessing.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [conceding] True. What about sustainability, then? All that re-using of costumes you were talking about?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [hesitant] I did think about that, but Dr Harmon said last year's group did exactly that topic, and she'd rather we didn't repeat it.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [thinking aloud] Right. Then how about how costume affects the way actors play a part? Remember Daniel saying he couldn't find his character until he'd put on those boots?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [enthusiastic] Yes! We've got loads of examples like that. Let's go with it.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [upbeat] Right, the section on tasks. Dyeing and ageing the fabric, the breaking down, was easily my favourite thing.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [wry] Not mine. I came home covered in dye every day. [short pause] But it'd be perfect for the final-year project, wouldn't it? Making a costume look as if it's been worn for years.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [decisive] Definitely. Let's put that down. We'll both build it into our projects.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [thoughtful] Fittings next. We'd sort of done measuring on the course, but only on each other, which isn't the same as dealing with a nervous actor at all.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [agreeing] No. And if we end up as wardrobe assistants, which is what we're both aiming for, that's what we'd be doing all day long.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: So it's directly relevant. Yes.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [doubtful] The running repairs during performances... I'd expected that to teach us a lot, you know, quick fixes under pressure.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [sighs] But it was mostly sewing buttons back on. It wasn't nearly as useful as I'd thought it would be.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Would you want more practice at it?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [laughs] Hardly. I've sewn on enough buttons for a lifetime.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [keen] Pattern cutting, though, that's different. We only ever got to watch Lorna doing it.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [eager] I know. I'd love to do a proper course in it. [hesitant] Could we use it in the project?

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [doubtful] Not unless we get a lot better at it first. It'd be far too ambitious. But yes, we should both ask the department about extra tuition.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [dismissive] And finally, the inventory. Logging every single costume in the database. I thought that was a complete waste of time.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [disagreeing] At first I did too. But when the director wanted that green cloak from three years ago, it took five minutes to find, purely because of the records.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [conceding slowly] OK, that's true. It's not that it was pointless. It's that nobody ever told us why we were doing it.

script.speaker: Freya
script.text: [decisive] Exactly. So we should recommend that next year's students get that explained at the start.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [relieved] Agreed. Right, I think that's the form done. Coffee?

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Ice Cores and Past Climate
parts.scenario: A lecturer in physical geography explains how glacier ice forms, how ice cores are dated and analysed, and what they reveal about past climate.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: University lecturer — male, 50s, authoritative, engaging, dry humour, measured pace; British RP (en-GB)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about how glaciers and ice cores record past climate. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, faint murmur fading] [clear, engaging] Good morning. Last week we looked at tree rings and lake sediments as records of past climate. Today I want to turn to what is, arguably, the richest archive of all, and that's the ice locked up in glaciers and ice sheets.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured, explaining] Let's start with how glacier ice actually forms. Snow that survives the summer melt is gradually buried by later falls, and under that weight it's compressed into a dense, granular material. You'll sometimes see the French word névé used for it, but the term glaciologists generally prefer is firn, that's F-I-R-N. Firn is no longer snow, but it isn't yet ice either.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [deliberate] Over decades, as the firn is pressed down further, the gaps between the grains close up, and the air in them is sealed off in tiny bubbles. [emphatic] And those bubbles are the key point. People sometimes imagine the old air is somehow dissolved into the ice. It isn't. It's physically trapped, as genuine samples of the ancient atmosphere.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful aside] One complication, incidentally: while the firn is still porous, air can circulate within it, so the gas in a bubble is always somewhat younger than the ice that surrounds it. We correct for that, but it's worth bearing in mind.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [brisk] So, how do we date an ice core? Near the top, we can simply count annual layers, rather like counting tree rings. Now, students often assume the layers show up because of differences in colour. [slight smile in voice] It isn't so much colour as dust. Snow that falls in spring and early summer contains a lot more of it, blown in from dry regions, so each year shows up as a slightly cloudier band.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [serious] Further down, though, the layers are squeezed so thin that counting becomes impossible. So we look for marker horizons. Large volcanic eruptions are ideal. You might expect us to look for ash, but ash rarely travels that far. What does reach the poles is acid, carried in the atmosphere and then deposited in the snow, and we can detect it by passing an electric current along the core.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] If we know the date of the eruption, from historical records for example, we have a fixed point in the core. The eruption of Tambora, in Indonesia, in eighteen fifteen is a classic example. It shows up clearly in cores from both poles, and it's linked in written accounts to the so-called year without a summer, when harvests failed across much of Europe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] Between these fixed points, we also use computer models of how ice flows and thins with depth. They're not perfect, and you'll find that published ages for the deepest ice can differ by several thousand years, depending on the team. But taken together, these methods give us a timescale we can have reasonable confidence in.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [clear, slowing slightly] Now to temperature. Water molecules come in slightly different weights, depending on which isotopes they contain. Isotopes of hydrogen are sometimes measured as a cross-check, but the standard measure is oxygen. Specifically, we look at the ratio of heavy oxygen to the normal, lighter form.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] The colder the air, the fewer heavy molecules make it as far as the ice sheet, so a lower ratio means a colder climate. It's an indirect method, but a remarkably reliable one.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [emphatic] Then there are the gases in those bubbles. Two in particular matter. Carbon dioxide, of course, and also methane, which is produced largely by wetlands, so it tells us a great deal about rainfall in the tropics. [dry] Nitrogen, by contrast, makes up most of the air in the bubbles, but since its level hardly changes, it's of very little use to us.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] What these gas records show, quite strikingly, is that carbon dioxide and temperature have risen and fallen together throughout the last eight hundred thousand years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [comparative] Where do the cores come from? The longest continuous record we have, covering roughly eight hundred thousand years, comes from Antarctica, where snowfall is so light that a great many years are packed into each metre. Greenland is different. Its cores cover a much shorter period, and they can't compete on length. What Greenland offers instead is detail. The heavier snowfall means each year's layer is thick enough to examine individually, even season by season.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [shifting focus] It isn't only the polar ice sheets that matter. High mountain glaciers, in the Andes and the Himalayas, for instance, preserve their own records. [qualifying] These are less useful for temperature than you might think, because local conditions vary so much. Their real value is as a record of rainfall, particularly the strength of the monsoon over past centuries.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [grave] Unfortunately, many of these glaciers are melting so fast that their records are being lost before we can study them. In the past, cores were simply sent to laboratory freezers, mostly in Europe and North America. But freezers fail, and funding runs out. So a recent international project has started storing duplicate cores in Antarctica, in a cave dug into the snow, where the temperature stays below minus fifty degrees without any machinery at all.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [looking ahead, enthusiastic] Finally, the frontier of the field. Several teams are now drilling in search of ice one and a half million years old. Why? Because at some point around a million years ago, the pattern of ice ages changed. [deliberate] They didn't become more frequent. In fact, the reverse is true. They became less frequent, but each one was longer and considerably more severe.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] Nobody yet knows why, and ice from that period may well hold the answer. [wrapping up] Next week we'll look at the methods used to drill and transport these cores, which is a story in itself.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
